input.title: Right-Ankle Running Rehabilitation History — January–April 2027
input.body:
Right-Ankle Running Rehabilitation History
January–April 2027

Prepared: January 1, 2028
Purpose: Historical chronology for clinician review

Important scope statement

This document records a historical, self-reported chronology of the right-ankle return-to-running rehabilitation described below. It is not a current examination, current clearance statement, or a new progression recommendation. The historical permissions and limits noted here applied at the time and should not be interpreted as applying now. Current activity decisions should come from the treating clinician’s present assessment.

Background entering January 2027

- December 26, 2026: During the third running interval of a prescribed 20-minute run-walk session, a focal ache inside the right ankle began, reported at approximately 2/10. The session was stopped; the ache settled in about 10 minutes. There was no swelling, instability, visible injury, or gait change, and necessary walking remained symptom-free.
- January 8, 2027 rehabilitation follow-up: The working assessment recorded in the contemporaneous history was load-sensitive medial ankle tendon irritation. The former two-session, 40-minute running baseline was suspended. The documented conditions for a future restart were 14 consecutive symptom-free days, followed by a symptom-free 30-minute brisk walk and following-day check. Ankle-and-calf strengthening was continued three times weekly.

January 2027: prerequisites and initial run-walk restart

January 23–24: prerequisite walking test

- January 23: Completed a 30-minute brisk walk after the required 14 consecutive symptom-free days. The test included a five-minute easy start, the 30-minute brisk walk, and a five-minute post-walk check.
- During the walk, later that day, and through January 24: No focal right-ankle pain or gait change was reported. Ordinary walking and stairs remained symptom-free.
- This walk was documented as a prerequisite, not as independent permission for continuous running.

Initial run-walk structure and spacing

- Frequency/spacing: Two nonconsecutive sessions per week, with no third weekly session.
- Session structure: 20 minutes total, alternating four-minute easy runs with one-minute walks; the documented format was four rounds of four-minute easy running alternating with one-minute walking.
- During-session stop rule: Stop for focal right-ankle pain or a gait change; do not push through a concerning symptom.
- Tolerance checks: Assess symptoms during the session, again later the same day, and through the following day, including ordinary walking and stairs.
- Boundary at this stage: Continuous running remained unapproved pending the required symptom-free sessions and clinical review.

Completed initial run-walk sessions

- January 26: 20-minute 4-minute-easy-run/1-minute-walk session. No focal ankle pain, swelling, instability, or gait change during the session or later that day. Ordinary walking and stairs remained symptom-free through January 27.
- January 30: Same 20-minute alternating structure. No focal ankle pain, swelling, instability, or gait change during the intervals or later that day. Ordinary walking and stairs remained symptom-free through January 31. Spacing from January 26: 4 days.
- February 2: Same 20-minute alternating structure. No focal ankle pain, swelling, instability, or gait change during the intervals or later that day. Ordinary walking and stairs remained symptom-free through February 3. Spacing from January 30: 3 days.
- February 6: Same 20-minute alternating structure; the session and following-day checks were recorded as symptom-free through February 7. Spacing from February 2: 4 days.
- February 10: Same 20-minute alternating structure; no focal pain, swelling, instability, gait change, or following-day symptoms were reported. Spacing from February 6: 4 days.
- February 13: Same 20-minute alternating structure; no focal pain, swelling, instability, gait change, or following-day symptoms were reported. Spacing from February 10: 3 days.

By February 13, six nonconsecutive 20-minute sessions and their following-day checks had remained symptom-free. The contemporaneous February 19 review then documented the next historical step: two nonconsecutive 25-minute sessions per week using alternating nine-minute easy runs and one-minute walks, with six symptom-free sessions at that level required before continuous running.

February–March 2027: 25-minute run-walk block

- Frequency/spacing: Two nonconsecutive sessions per week; no third weekly session.
- Session structure: 25 minutes total using the prescribed alternating nine-minute easy-run/one-minute-walk pattern. The historical record does not add a new interval count beyond that prescribed pattern.
- Checks: Symptoms were assessed during the session, later that day, and through the following day, including ordinary walking and stairs.
- Continuing background: Ankle-and-calf strengthening continued three times weekly. The former 40-minute running baseline remained suspended during this block.

Six completed 25-minute sessions

- February 21: Symptom-free during the session, later that day, and the following day.
- February 24: Same prescribed structure and symptom-free session, later-day, and following-day checks. Spacing from February 21: 3 days.
- February 28: Same prescribed structure and symptom-free checks. Spacing from February 24: 4 days.
- March 3: Same prescribed structure and symptom-free checks. Spacing from February 28: 3 days.
- March 7: Same prescribed structure and symptom-free checks. Spacing from March 3: 4 days.
- March 10: Same prescribed structure; symptom-free during the session and later that day, with ordinary walking and stairs symptom-free through March 11. Spacing from March 7: 3 days.

The six-session 25-minute evidence requirement was complete by March 10–11. Continuous running was still held pending the March 15 clinical check.

March 2027: transition to continuous easy running

- March 15 clinical check: The historical record states that, after six symptom-free nonconsecutive 25-minute run-walk sessions, the clinician cleared two nonconsecutive 30-minute continuous easy runs per week. Ankle-and-calf strengthening and the session-plus-following-day symptom check continued. Forty-minute runs and a third weekly session were not included in that historical clearance.
- March 17: First documented post-check 30-minute continuous easy run. No focal ankle pain, swelling, instability, or gait change during the run or later that day. Ordinary walking and stairs remained symptom-free through the March 18 following-day check. Spacing from March 15 review: 2 days.
- March 21: Second documented 30-minute continuous easy run, nonconsecutive with March 17. No focal ankle pain, swelling, instability, or gait change during the run or later that day. Ordinary walking and stairs remained symptom-free through the March 22 following-day check. Spacing from March 17: 4 days.
- March 24: Continued at 30 minutes rather than increasing duration. No focal ankle pain, swelling, instability, or gait change during the run or later that day. Ordinary walking and stairs remained symptom-free through March 25. Spacing from March 21: 3 days.

April 2027: later 30-minute continuous-run block

- Frequency/spacing: Two nonconsecutive 30-minute continuous easy runs per week. No third weekly run was added. Duration was held at 30 minutes; no 40-minute run was attempted during this April block.
- Session structure: Continuous easy running for 30 minutes, without run-walk intervals. Ankle-and-calf strengthening continued three times weekly.
- During-session and later-day checks: For each run, the record reports no focal right-ankle pain, swelling, instability, or gait change during the run or later that day.
- Following-day checks: Ordinary walking and stairs remained symptom-free through the following-day check for every listed April run.

April sessions

- April 4: 30-minute continuous easy run. No listed ankle symptoms during or later that day; following-day ordinary walking and stairs were symptom-free.
- April 7: 30-minute continuous easy run. No listed ankle symptoms during or later that day; following-day ordinary walking and stairs were symptom-free. Spacing from April 4: 3 days.
- April 11: 30-minute continuous easy run. No listed ankle symptoms during or later that day; following-day ordinary walking and stairs were symptom-free. Spacing from April 7: 4 days.
- April 14: 30-minute continuous easy run. No listed ankle symptoms during or later that day; ordinary walking and stairs remained symptom-free through the April 15 check. Spacing from April 11: 3 days.

At the April 15 historical log correction, all four April runs were reported as clean through their same-day and following-day checks. The record also states that no 40-minute run and no third weekly session had been attempted.

Condensed chronology

- January 23–24: Symptom-free 30-minute brisk-walk prerequisite and following-day walking/stair check.
- January 26–February 13: Six nonconsecutive 20-minute run-walk sessions using 4-minute easy runs alternating with 1-minute walks; all documented session and following-day checks were symptom-free.
- February 21–March 10: Six nonconsecutive 25-minute run-walk sessions using 9-minute easy runs alternating with 1-minute walks; all documented session and following-day checks were symptom-free.
- March 15: Historical clinical review after the six-session 25-minute block.
- March 17–March 24: 30-minute continuous easy running remained symptom-free during, later the same day, and through following-day walking/stair checks.
- April 4–April 14: Four 30-minute continuous easy runs, spaced nonconsecutively at 3–4-day intervals, with no reported focal ankle pain, swelling, instability, or gait change during or later that day and symptom-free ordinary walking and stairs through each following-day check.

Clinician-facing interpretation of the record

The chronology shows a staged return from a January run-walk restart to a later April 30-minute continuous-run block. At each stage, the reported monitoring included during-session symptoms, later-that-day symptoms, and next-day function with ordinary walking and stairs. The record describes historical activity tolerance only. It does not establish the patient’s status on January 1, 2028, does not substitute for a current examination, and does not recommend continuing, resuming, extending, or otherwise changing running without current clinician direction.

  slice        n     by D0     by D3     by D7     by D14     median day
  churny       —       —         —         —         —           —
  retained     —       —         —         —         —           —
  difference   —       —         —         —         —           —

- D0
- D1–3
- D4–7
- D8–14

# Mid-segment churn investigation: H1–H4 hypothesis crosswalk

Archived investigation window: Feb–Apr 2023
Canonical source: “Mid-segment churn investigation Feb-Apr 2023 -- what we learned”

Purpose: Preserve the original numbering used in the investigation. Later references to H1–H4 decode as follows; the numbers were not renumbered as hypotheses were ruled out.

| ID | Original hypothesis | What the number refers to | Investigation read |
|---|---|---|---|
| H1 | Pricing artifact | Packaging, discounting, contract-mix, or tier effects; separate from Marcus’s pricing-page experiment | Ruled out: Entry / Standard / Plus churn was essentially flat (5.0% / 5.2% / 5.1%; about 20 bps spread). |
| H2 | Competitor cycle | A competitor action or a generic seasonal cycle caused the February spike | Ruled out: same-cohort February churn was 2.0% in 2021 and 2.2% in 2022, with no comparable spike. |
| H3 | Onboarding timing | Late-December / early-January starts converted to churn on a lag because first value or the onboarding touch arrived too late | Supported by the activation-triggered onboarding test: pooled week-1 retention +3.1 points versus control (p=0.04, n=420 across two cohorts); full rollout began Apr 10. Later reads treated the Apr 17–20 wobble as a one-time CS auto-onboarding-nudge outage / timing artifact, not a regression in the trigger. |
| H4 | CS coverage gap | CSM load or coverage drift explained the spike | The original fourth hypothesis; retain this number and label in any later reference. Do not reinterpret H4 as the Apr 17 trigger wobble: that incident was documented separately as the CS auto-onboarding-nudge outage. |

Numbering rule

- H1 = pricing artifact
- H2 = competitor cycle
- H3 = onboarding timing
- H4 = CS coverage gap

Do not renumber after H1 or H2 were ruled out. “Two down, two left” meant H1/H2 were closed while H3/H4 remained the numbered board items.

Scope note: The original investigation used the v1 mid-segment definition (50–200 seats) for its early cuts and later defaulted to v2 (75–200 seats), retaining v1 only for comparisons. This cohort-definition change does not change H1–H4 numbering.

Subject: Helio Start: instrumentation gate for pricing-page work

Daniela’s engineering scoping clarified the sequencing for Helio Start. A pricing-page redesign is feasible, but our current funnel events cannot reliably distinguish self-serve-eligible accounts from sales- or CS-assisted accounts.

Before we use a customer-facing pricing-page change for measurement or launch decisions, we need an instrumentation gate cleared:

- Event taxonomy that identifies the relevant funnel stages and account path
- Entitlement instrumentation
- Clean properties for admin complexity, import/migration help, support handoff, and entitlement state

This belongs on the operating-model critical path. It is not a request to stop design exploration. Design can continue with content, packaging, and layout concepts; the constraint is on changing the live pricing-page or signup layout in the same measurement window as the taxonomy, dashboard, or entitlement changes. We should sequence those changes separately so the eventual read remains interpretable.

input.title: Helio Start change-sequencing checklist — 2028-01-01
input.body:
Purpose

Sequence Helio Start changes so that customer-facing work does not outrun eligibility, operating-model, billing, or measurement decisions. “Helio Start” remains a scenario/label for the bounded sub-50-seat motion unless the applicable readiness decision says otherwise.

Checklist

1. Packaging

Settle first:

- Eligibility rules: define the qualifying customer/account shape, including seat band, deployment shape, and the self-serve boundary.
- Refusal and assisted-routing rules: decide which cases must be refused or routed to Sales/CS rather than packaged as self-serve. Keep billing exceptions, manual import/migration needs, unsupported permissions, and unresolved ownership in this decision.
- Customer-protective language and the support handoff path: establish what the package promises and what it explicitly does not promise.

Blocks downstream:

- Packaging names, inclusions, exclusions, entitlement promises, and customer-facing copy.
- Any pricing-page or signup claim about who can use Helio Start.
- Lifecycle automation that would treat an ineligible or assisted account as a self-serve customer.
- Meaningful packaging readouts: without settled eligibility/refusal rules, the cohort and denominator are not interpretable.

Can proceed in parallel:

- Internal scenario titles, label exploration, and non-live design concepts. Do not convert the working name into public pricing-page copy or imply launch timing.

2. Pricing-page experiment

Settle first:

- Event taxonomy and funnel stages that identify the account path.
- Canonical entitlement instrumentation and a QA-clean entitlement path.
- Clean properties for admin complexity, import/migration help, support handoff, and entitlement state; use import_help_requested where it is already reliably captured.
- Billing sign-off.
- A clean baseline and experiment design, including the eligible self-serve denominator and the assisted/refused paths.
- The change window: do not ship a live pricing-page or signup-layout change in the same measurement window as taxonomy, dashboard, or entitlement changes.

Blocks downstream:

- Customer-facing pricing-page exposure, signup-layout exposure, and any launch decision based on the experiment.
- Reliable separation of self-serve-eligible accounts from Sales- or CS-assisted accounts.
- Interpretable conversion, checkout, and activation readouts.
- Any claim that a pricing-page result supports a broader launch, pipeline, or revenue conclusion.

Hard stop:

- Do not substitute manually maintained spreadsheet tags for entitlement instrumentation.
- Do not expose the pricing-page change before the measurement path is clean, Billing has signed off, and the entitlement path is QA-clean.

3. Paid acquisition

Settle first:

- Lifecycle fork: define the onboarding/lifecycle path for Helio Start separately from existing retained-mid and other motions, including assisted routing and support boundaries.
- Eligibility, refusal, and fail-closed behavior must be operational—not merely documented—before paid traffic can create a comparable cohort.
- A separate paid experiment brief with explicit spend, attribution, cohort-quality criteria, support-capacity/economics measures, and stop rules.
- Evidence gate: first-paid and day-90 retention evidence must be available before reconsidering paid acquisition or a pipeline target; organic Helio Start evidence does not by itself authorize paid spend.
- Approval for the paid batch and its budget. Paid acquisition is not implied by packaging, a pricing-page experiment, or a controlled beta.

Blocks downstream:

- Any paid traffic, paid batch, acquisition forecast, or pipeline target.
- Causal attribution of paid acquisition to qualified, supportable Helio Start accounts.
- Paid-cohort quality, paid support economics, and stop/go interpretation.
- Treating organic pricing-page performance or controlled-beta activation as evidence that paid acquisition will scale.

Sequencing rule:

- Lifecycle fork before paid acquisition. Keep Helio Start as a bounded organic channel until the evidence and approvals above clear; do not run paid acquisition concurrently with an unresolved lifecycle or eligibility fork.

4. Activation measurement

Settle first:

- Activation definition v3 and the event/instrumentation contract, including the timing and canonical entitlement state used to establish cohort membership.
- Helio Start eligibility and cohort assignment: keep the sub-50-seat/deployment-shape/eligibility fields explicit in measurement tables.
- Support and handoff-state handling: represent unresolved support state as pending rather than as a real state; exclude pending rows from support-dependent activation cuts until resolved.
- Reporting denominators and cuts, including activation, first integration, support-load mix, and handoff quality.
- A separate controlled-beta learning/readout frame—not a revenue motion.

Blocks downstream:

- Activation dashboards, beta readouts, lifecycle decisions, and support-capacity interpretation.
- Comparisons that claim Helio Start performance is equivalent to another customer population.
- Any revenue, retention, or launch inference from activation results.

Required population separation

- Report Helio Start activation in its own beta cohort and readout.
- Keep it separate from the retained mid-segment (the 75–200-seat mid-seg baseline), and do not merge its metrics or denominators with retained-mid.
- Keep it separate from Expansion Assist as well; do not merge populations, metrics, or denominators.
- Show the 50–75-seat band separately rather than silently assigning it to either Helio Start or retained-mid.
- Keep checklist exposure, admission outcomes, and activation outcomes as separate measures; checklist exposure must not be used as a proxy for admission or activation.
- If paid acquisition is later approved, report the paid cohort separately from organic Helio Start and evaluate it with its own attribution, maturity, cash, support, and stop-rule fields.

Release order

1. Settle eligibility, refusal, assisted-routing, and support boundaries.
2. Settle packaging and entitlement meaning.
3. Instrument and QA the event taxonomy, entitlement path, billing path, and required properties.
4. Define activation v3, cohort assignment, denominators, pending-state handling, and the separated reporting views.
5. Run any pricing-page experiment in a distinct change window after the measurement path is clean.
6. Complete the lifecycle fork and obtain the separate paid-experiment evidence/approval gate before any paid acquisition.

Final gate

No change is ready merely because its design is complete. The applicable prerequisite must be settled, its downstream dependency verified, and the affected measurement population preserved as a distinct cohort.

- Completed the prescribed first 15-minute continuous easy run on the morning lake trail.

- Reduced-load continuous easy run with no pace or distance target; stop for focal inside-right-ankle ache or any change in gait, then check symptoms during the following day.

Contained migration plan: `is_test` to `workspace_environment`

Objective

Move measurement and lifecycle logic from the legacy `is_test` field to the required `workspace_environment` value without changing cohort definitions, allowing sandbox data into production reads, or creating a discontinuity in Helio Start or ordinary onboarding metrics.

The migration should be treated as an instrumentation and query-semantics change, not as a product or lifecycle experiment. Helio Start remains a capped, manually controlled cohort with its activation read separate from ordinary Starter onboarding.

1. Freeze the contract before February 12

Daniela should document and lock:

- Allowed values: `production`, `sandbox`.
- The exact cutover timestamp and timezone.
- Whether the value is supplied by the producer, the workspace registry, or both.
- The rule for imported events and replayed events.
- The producer/schema version that indicates the new contract is active.
- Behavior for missing, invalid, or conflicting values.

The cutover must be based on ingestion/schema version, not event timestamp alone. A historical event replayed after February 12 must not be treated as a new-schema event merely because it arrived later.

Raw fields should remain immutable:

- Preserve `is_test` on historical rows.
- Preserve `workspace_environment` on new rows.
- Do not backfill `is_test` onto post-cutover imported events.
- Do not overwrite a source value to make the two fields agree.

2. Add a normalized dual-read layer

Create a versioned compatibility view or derived field, for example:

`resolved_workspace_environment_v1`

Resolution rules:

1. If the event is on the new schema and has `workspace_environment` equal to `production` or `sandbox`, use that value.
2. If a historical row has no new-schema environment but has `is_test`:
   - `is_test = true` → `sandbox`
   - `is_test = false` → `production`
3. If both fields exist and disagree, return `conflict`; do not silently choose one.
4. If a post-cutover event has no valid `workspace_environment`, return `unknown`; do not infer `production`.
5. Invalid values, missing workspace identity, and ambiguous workspace mappings also return `unknown` or `conflict`, with a reason code.

Example derived fields:

```text
resolved_workspace_environment
environment_source
environment_resolution_status
environment_resolution_reason
```

Suggested reason codes:

```text
new_schema_value
legacy_is_test_mapping
field_conflict
missing_post_cutover_environment
invalid_environment
missing_workspace
ambiguous_workspace_mapping
```

The old and new interpretations should be exposed side by side during the migration:

```text
legacy_environment
resolved_workspace_environment
legacy_activation_result
dual_read_activation_result
legacy_lifecycle_eligibility
dual_read_lifecycle_eligibility
discrepancy_reason
```

This gives Owen and Ines a row-level diff rather than only aggregate totals.

3. Change consumers in two phases

Phase A: shadow reads, no behavioral change

Update these consumers to calculate both paths:

- Activation definition v3.
- Lifecycle eligibility query 1.
- Lifecycle eligibility query 2.

During this phase:

- Existing lifecycle sends remain governed by the currently approved production behavior.
- The new query results are logged but do not trigger sends or state changes.
- No new suppression, invitation, reminder, or support-routing behavior is enabled.
- Any `unknown` or `conflict` row is excluded from eligibility and placed on an audit list.
- Helio Start and ordinary onboarding remain separate dashboard sections with separate denominators.

For activation v3, the new path must retain the existing semantics:

- Count a real first integration and data flow.
- Do not count `template_imported` as a first integration.
- Preserve the product-seen guardrail.
- Preserve any existing ordering/provisional treatment around entitlement state.
- Exclude sandbox activity wherever the current production measurement excludes `is_test = true`.

For lifecycle eligibility, the new path must preserve:

- Existing workspace and account scope.
- Existing eligibility and refusal rules.
- Existing support-handoff exclusions.
- Existing suppression and duplicate-send behavior.
- Existing unsupported-path handling.
- No production-only branch may qualify a sandbox workspace.
- No missing or conflicting environment may qualify for a send.

Phase B: controlled decision cutover

After the acceptance checks pass, switch the consumers to `resolved_workspace_environment_v1`.

The cutover should be reversible through a feature flag or query-version selector:

```text
measurement_environment_reader = legacy | dual_read | resolved_v1
lifecycle_environment_reader = legacy | dual_read | resolved_v1
```

The fallback must be to hold ambiguous records, not to reinterpret missing post-cutover values as production.

4. Production-versus-sandbox equivalence test

Use paired fixtures and replayed events with identical attributes except for environment.

For each fixture, test:

- Same workspace/account shape.
- Same integration type.
- Same event ordering.
- Same entitlement state.
- Same support state.
- Same lifecycle history.
- One version marked `production`.
- One version marked `sandbox`.

Expected behavior:

- The event parses identically in both environments.
- The integration event is counted or rejected for the same semantic reasons.
- Only the intentional environment predicate differs.
- A sandbox event cannot satisfy a production-only activation or lifecycle condition.
- A production event is not dropped merely because `is_test` is absent.
- A sandbox event is not treated as production because `is_test` is absent.
- The same event sequence does not create duplicate activation or duplicate lifecycle eligibility.
- Environment is carried through to the final lifecycle send decision, not only applied during audience construction.

Test at least these cases:

```text
1. Historical production row:
   is_test = false, no workspace_environment

2. Historical sandbox row:
   is_test = true, no workspace_environment

3. Post-cutover production import:
   workspace_environment = production, no is_test

4. Post-cutover sandbox import:
   workspace_environment = sandbox, no is_test

5. Both fields agree:
   is_test = false, workspace_environment = production

6. Both fields conflict:
   is_test = true, workspace_environment = production

7. Post-cutover missing environment

8. Invalid environment value

9. Replayed historical event received after cutover

10. Same email/contact associated with production and sandbox workspaces
```

The conflict, missing, and invalid cases must be held or excluded and must appear in an operational exception report.

5. Acceptance checks

A. Schema and instrumentation checks

Go only if all of the following pass:

- Every new-schema `integration_connected` event has `workspace_environment` populated.
- Every populated value is exactly `production` or `sandbox`.
- No new-schema event relies on an `is_test` backfill.
- Historical `is_test` mappings are complete or explicitly classified as unknown.
- No workspace maps simultaneously to production and sandbox without an explicit multi-environment model.
- Conflicting fields are observable and never silently resolved.
- Raw source fields remain unchanged.
- Event ordering and deduplication behavior are unchanged.
- Daniela’s QA sample confirms the event taxonomy and workspace mapping.

B. Historical equivalence checks

Run the legacy and resolved readers across a pre-cutover window, including historical Helio Start and ordinary Starter cohorts.

Required result:

- Activation-v3 eligible IDs are exactly equal between the two readers, except for discrepancies individually explained by a documented legacy anomaly.
- Both lifecycle eligible ID sets are exactly equal, or every difference has a disposition before cutover.
- No unexplained change in activation numerator or denominator.
- No unexplained change in lifecycle audience size.
- No discontinuity at the day or cohort boundary around February 12.
- Historical comparisons remain calculated under activation definition v3, not a mixed v2/v3 or mixed environment definition.

Aggregate equality is not sufficient. Require row-level comparison because offsetting false positives and false negatives could leave totals unchanged.

C. Helio Start protection checks

Helio Start must pass separately from ordinary onboarding:

- The Helio Start cohort remains capped and unchanged.
- Helio Start workspaces retain their existing eligibility, entitlement, and support-state classifications.
- No sandbox workspace enters a production-only Helio Start activation read.
- No production Helio Start workspace is lost because `is_test` is absent.
- No `unknown` or `conflict` environment is treated as eligible.
- First-integration logic remains the real integration path; `template_imported` remains non-activating.
- Helio Start activation is not blended into the ordinary Starter denominator.
- The migration does not create a new invite, exposure, paid-acquisition, pricing-page, or launch implication.

D. Ordinary onboarding checks

For normal onboarding:

- Activation definition v3 produces the same cohort membership before and after the reader switch.
- Production imports with no `is_test` backfill are included correctly.
- Sandbox imports are excluded or handled exactly as the prior production rule intended.
- Denominators remain visible and stable.
- The ordinary Starter trend has no artificial February 12 step change.
- Any immature or incomplete cohort remains labeled as immature rather than interpreted as a product movement.

E. Lifecycle safety checks

Before enabling the new reader for sends:

- Both lifecycle eligibility queries have row-level equality or documented exceptions.
- Unknown, invalid, and conflict rows are held.
- No sandbox contact is eligible for a production-only message.
- No production contact is omitted solely because `is_test` is null.
- Duplicate-send checks pass across retries, workflow re-entry, backfills, and audience refreshes.
- Suppression and support-handoff exclusions remain unchanged.
- Message decisions retain workspace context through the final send gate.
- A dry-run send report shows zero unexpected additions and zero unexplained removals.

- Keep the old field available for historical audit and rollback until the agreed retention period ends.

Owen must sign off on the measurement contract:

- First integration and product-seen guardrails are unchanged.

Ines must sign off on the lifecycle contract:

- Production and sandbox scope is correct for every affected message path.
- Missing, invalid, or conflicting environment values are held, not promoted to production.
- No duplicate sends or suppression regressions occur.
- Workspace context survives through final send evaluation.
- Unsupported, assisted, and support-handoff paths remain excluded.
- The new reader is shadow-tested and the dry-run audience has no unexplained additions or removals.

Daniela should provide the technical instrumentation sign-off:

- The event contract is enforced.
- Raw fields are preserved.

- Rollback is tested.

Retirement rule

Do not retire the old field merely because the new query returns plausible totals.

Retire legacy reads only after Owen and Ines have both signed off, Daniela has confirmed instrumentation integrity, and the monitoring window has completed without unexplained discrepancies.

Even then:

- Retire `is_test` as a consumer field first.

- Drop or archive the column only after the retention period and final historical-read validation are complete.

input.title: Warehouse Glossary — Activation Definition v2 (Historical)
input.body:
Activation definition v2

Status: Historical / retired from the metric of record. Retain for historical analyses and explicitly named comparison series. Do not use as the default definition for new activation reporting.

Exact criteria

An account is activated under v2 if and only if both conditions are met within 14 days of the cohort anchor:

- The account completes its first integration.
- The account logs in at least twice within the same 14-day window.

Canonical shorthand: first integration + logged in twice in 14 days.

The login requirement is a minimum threshold: two or more logins, not exactly two. The first-integration and login conditions are conjunctive; satisfying only one condition does not qualify the account. Do not substitute v3’s qualifying in-product event for the v2 login requirement, and do not relabel a v2 result as v3.

Active-cut period

- Active beginning: November 2022. Historical records identify v2 as the cut in use since November 2022.
- Replacement: Activation definition v3 was shipped in March 2023; the March 16, 2023 warehouse decision records v3 as shipping now and v2 as remaining in the warehouse.
- Exact retirement timestamp for v2 as the active cut: not recorded in the available history. Therefore, the defensible period label is “November 2022 through the v3 replacement/cutover in March 2023,” rather than an invented end date.
- Later historical views may still show v2 because older notebooks or analyses were not automatically rewritten; that is a definition/version difference, not evidence of a product change.

Replacement context

The successor activation definition v3 uses completed first integration plus at least one qualifying in-product event inside 14 days. It replaced the UI-shaped “two logins” gate with a product-use signal. V2 and v3 are not interchangeable and can produce different activation rates for the same cohort.

Warehouse handling after replacement

- Preserve v2 as a separately named, versioned historical definition and comparison series.
- Do not delete v2 tables, rows, labels, or historical values.
- Do not overwrite or backfill historical v2 results with v3 results.
- Label every v2 output with the definition version, 14-day window, cohort basis, and data freshness.
- Use v2 only when reproducing the historical cut, reconciling an older notebook or report, or presenting an explicitly labeled comparison series.
- Use v3 as the metric of record for new activation work unless a later approved definition supersedes it.
- When comparing v2 with v3, state that the views use different activation definitions; do not interpret the difference alone as product performance movement.
- Keep versioned warehouse tables/query logic available so historical cohort comparisons remain reproducible and auditable.

Source note

The historical record states: v2 was “first integration + logged in twice in 14 days” from November 2022; v3 was shipped in March 2023; and all three definitions were to remain in versioned warehouse tables. The exact calendar day on which v2 ceased to be the active cut is not specified, so this note intentionally preserves that uncertainty.

results.content:
Card fee notice and benefit summary:
The annual fee changes from $95 to $150 on April 15, 2025. I redeemed $218 in points, used the full $75 annual travel credit, and used two lounge passes in the prior twelve months. The advertised no-fee product change preserves existing points, earns 1.5x on travel and dining, and removes the travel credit and lounge passes. The notice does not state the downgrade deadline or annual-fee refund rule.

Using the terms previously recorded:

- Annual-fee card: $150 annual fee
- Travel credit: $75, if fully usable
- No-fee card: $0 annual fee
- No-fee earning rate: 1.5x on travel and dining
- Annual-fee card: higher travel/dining rate, but the exact rate is not in the information I have
- Annual-fee card: two lounge passes
- Previously redeemed $218 in points: excluded, because it is a one-time historical value rather than a recurring annual benefit

Net annual cost before valuing points or lounge access

Option                         Fee       Credit       Net annual cost
Annual-fee card, credit used   $150      −$75         $75
Annual-fee card, no credit     $150      $0           $150
No-fee card                    $0        $0           $0

Therefore, the annual-fee card has an incremental annual cost of:

- $75 if the full travel credit is used
- $150 if the credit is not used

Break-even value per extra point

Let:

- L = your value for the two lounge passes
- B = any other quantifiable incremental value from the annual-fee card
- S = annual travel/dining spending receiving the higher rate
- r = annual-fee card’s earning rate
- The no-fee card’s rate = 1.5x

The annual-fee card’s extra points are:

(r − 1.5) × S

With the full $75 credit:

Break-even value per extra point =
($75 − L − B) ÷ [(r − 1.5) × S]

Without using the credit:

Break-even value per extra point =
($150 − L − B) ÷ [(r − 1.5) × S]

If lounge passes and other benefits are assigned no value, the hurdle is simply:

$75 ÷ extra points, if the credit is used

or

$150 ÷ extra points, if it is not used

Illustrations, assuming no value assigned to lounges or other benefits:

Premium rate    Eligible spend    Extra points    Value needed per extra point
2x              $5,000             2,500           3.00 cents
2x              $10,000            5,000           1.50 cents
3x              $5,000             7,500           1.00 cent
3x              $10,000            15,000          0.50 cents

Those examples are conditional because the premium card’s exact rate is not recorded here. The correct spending base is only the travel/dining spending for which the premium card earns more than 1.5x.

For example, if the two lounge passes are worth $30 total and the full credit is used, the extra-points hurdle falls from $75 to $45. At $5,000 of eligible spending:

- At 2x versus 1.5x: $45 ÷ 2,500 = 1.8 cents per extra point
- At 3x versus 1.5x: $45 ÷ 7,500 = 0.6 cents per extra point

Nonquantified tradeoffs

Annual-fee card advantages:

- Lounge access convenience, particularly during delays or long connections
- Travel protections, potentially including trip cancellation/interruption, delay, baggage, and rental-car coverage
- Purchase protections, extended warranty, return protection, or cellphone coverage
- Potentially better transfer partners, redemption flexibility, or rewards-related features
- Possible concierge, hotel, or other card-linked services
- Retaining the option to use premium benefits without buying separate lounge access or coverage

No-fee card advantages:

- No fixed annual cost and no need to manufacture spending to use a credit
- Simpler economics and less risk that a benefit expires unused
- Existing points remain preserved under the recorded product-change terms
- Lower exposure to changes in lounge availability, eligibility, capacity, or guest rules
- Less dependence on travel volume or on transactions qualifying under narrow credit rules
- Potentially simpler account management and fewer benefit terms to monitor

Operational or uncertain tradeoffs to verify separately:

- Whether the higher-rate card’s travel and dining categories exclude transit, rideshare, third-party bookings, or particular merchants
- Lounge network, guest access, capacity restrictions, expiration, and whether unused passes disappear immediately on conversion
- Whether travel protections apply only when the trip is paid for with that card
- Whether the product change preserves the account number, credit line, account age, autopay arrangements, digital-wallet tokens, and authorized users
- Any difference in foreign-transaction fees, APR, balance-transfer terms, or redemption restrictions
- Whether the annual fee is charged upfront while the credit posts later, creating a cash-flow difference
- Whether changing products can be reversed later
- Whether the issuer changes transfer partners, point expiration rules, redemption rates, or reward eligibility

The clean quantitative threshold is therefore $75 of incremental annual value when the credit is fully used, or $150 when it is not. The extra points must make up whatever remains after assigning values to the lounge passes and any other incremental benefits.

sources.label: Assistant's reply to Riley Tanaka, message 000960
excerpts:
January 11 — Investigation-framework practice intro
Audience: Growth and Customer Success leads
Length: 25 minutes

Objective

Teach a lightweight set of decision rules that teams can reuse in experiment, retention, and renewal investigations:

1. Show the denominator, cohort, metric, and time window.
2. Show the observed effect size—and, where relevant, the decision-relevant threshold.
3. Put the conclusion after the evidence.
4. Treat first significance as a signal, not a rollout decision; wait for a stabilization cohort.
5. Check lifecycle and audience risk before proposing a customer-facing action.

Timed agenda

0:00–2:00 — Opening: purpose and scope
Owner: Riley

Set the frame:

- This is a practical readout habit, not a new approval process.
- The goal is to make decision rules visible and reusable.
- The practice is the Q1 default for Growth and Customer Success, while teams retain judgment and can adapt the format to fit the work.
- Owen and Ines own review lenses, not approval of every readout.

2:00–7:00 — Owen: make the evidence travel with the conclusion
Length: 5 minutes

Owen’s role: standard readout shape and effect-size placement.

Suggested structure:

- Start with the denominator: who was included, cohort definition, metric, and time window.
- State the observed effect size before describing what it means.
- Distinguish observed effect size from the minimum effect that would change the decision.
- Put the conclusion last, after the evidence and its limitations.
- Label the decision status clearly: first significance, stabilization-cohort confirmation, or observation that should not drive action yet.

Usable rule:

“Do not make the audience infer the size, reliability, or decision status of the result from a conclusion.”

7:00–10:00 —

input.title: Historical framing note — Mid-segment churn investigation (Feb–Apr 2023)
input.body:
This investigation began on February 7, 2023, after a validated mid-segment monthly-churn reading of 5.1% versus a 2.1% trailing-six-month baseline. The work was deliberately kept separate from the concurrent pricing-page experiment so the team could test the signal and its competing explanations without parallel-experiment noise.

Across February through April, the investigation ruled out a pricing-tier artifact, tested the onboarding-trigger hypothesis, and waited for a stabilization cohort before treating the improvement as durable. The reporting definition was then refined from the legacy 50–200-seat bucket to the 75–200-seat v2 cohort, with historicals backfilled for comparison. By April 30, v2 monthly churn was 3.8%; the backfilled comparison supported genuine recovery, not merely a bucket-definition change. The completed record is preserved as “Mid-segment churn investigation Feb-Apr 2023 -- what we learned,” a factual reference for future analyses rather than a postmortem or a mandate to reuse the process unchanged.

Do not reuse the stale cohort logic from the April 2023 read.

Corrected cohort boundary: mid-segment v2 is paid accounts with 75–200 seats. The historical 50–200-seat v1 cut is retained only for comparison; the 50–75-seat accounts are not part of the corrected cohort.

Why the original read was noisy:
- Classification issue: the segment job misclassified some 50–75-seat accounts as mid-segment, inflating and mis-composing the denominator before retention was calculated.
- Timing issue: the onboarding send read stale segment membership during the cache window. Separately, the CS auto-onboarding nudge outage delayed activation for affected accounts; the downstream activation-event email still sent, but at a different point in the onboarding flow. Treat the resulting April 17 dip as a timing artifact, not evidence that the trigger’s conversion logic failed.

Use the 75–200-seat boundary and account for cache/send timing in any retrospective or future comparison.

Owen should restructure the report into separate Start-only lanes. The key correction is that activation must not define the support denominator.

1. Cohort and maturity

Keep the intake and outcome cohorts distinct:

- Intake/routing cohort: all 120 Helio Start applications.
- Admitted eligible-start cohort: 104 starts admitted to the self-serve Start path.
- Mature outcome denominator: admitted eligible starts whose full seven-day observation window is complete.
- Still observing: admitted starts without a complete seven-day window; show separately and do not classify them as nonactivating or unsupported.

If all 104 admitted starts are mature, the outcome denominator is 104. If not, replace 104 with the mature count and keep the immature count visible.

2. Activation

Define activation as first integration by day seven:

Activation rate
= eligible starts with first integration by day 7
÷ mature eligible Start starts

Using the closed cohort:

- 68 activated / 104 mature eligible starts
- 36 / 104 did not integrate by day seven

The 36 nonactivating starts remain in the denominator. They must not be removed because they failed to activate, needed support before activation, or did not create a workspace.

Report the funnel steps separately:

- 104 eligible starts
- 82 created a workspace
- 68 reached first integration by day seven
- 36 did not reach first integration by day seven

Do not use “activated workspaces” as the denominator for any cohort-level rate.

3. Support load

Use two clearly labeled, non-additive cuts.

A. Overall eligible-Start support incidence

This is the cut that fixes Owen’s current error:

Eligible starts with at least one customer-initiated support contact
÷ mature eligible Start starts

The numerator includes eligible starts that requested help before activation. A start does not have to activate to remain in the denominator.

Also show contact volume:

Total customer-initiated support contacts
÷ mature eligible Start starts

This preserves repeat work without confusing contact count with workspace incidence.

B. Post-workspace support experience

For support specifically arising after workspace creation:

Created workspaces with at least one post-creation customer support contact
÷ mature created workspaces

And separately:

Post-workspace customer contacts
÷ mature created workspaces

The denominator is created workspaces, not activated workspaces. This is the experience among accounts that reached workspace setup; it is not the overall Start supportability rate.

Any unresolved support-state record should be labeled “pending support state,” excluded from support-dependent rates until resolved, and retained as a measurement exception rather than treated as “no support.”

4. Routed before setup

Keep routed-before-setup cases in the intake/routing lane, not in the admitted self-serve outcome denominator.

Routed-before-setup rate
= starts routed to Customer Success before workspace setup
÷ all Start intake applications or accepted Start invitations, whichever Owen defines as the fixed intake denominator

For the closed cohort:

- 16 routed out / 120 applications
- 13.3% of the intake cohort

Those cases should have:

- Their own count and rate
- Their reason category: agency identity, unresolved ownership, manual billing, import, migration, or other refusal condition
- Their CS workload and contacts shown separately
- Zero self-serve activation attributed to them unless they later enter the admitted Start path through a separately defined process

Do not silently delete them because they did not create a workspace, and do not fold them into post-workspace support. They are routing and operating-capacity demand, not admitted self-serve setup failures.

5. Nonactivating eligible starts

Create an explicit row:

Nonactivating eligible starts
= mature eligible Start starts − starts with first integration by day seven

Rate:

Nonactivating eligible starts
÷ mature eligible Start starts

For the closed cohort:

- 36 nonactivating / 104 eligible starts
- 34.6%

Label this “not integrated by day seven,” not “failed,” unless the report has a separately defined failure diagnosis. The row includes eligible starts that created a workspace but never integrated, as well as eligible starts that did not reach workspace setup. Do not exclude either group.

- 120 intake applications
  - 104 admitted eligible Start starts
  - 16 routed before setup
- 104 mature eligible Start starts
  - 68 integrated by day seven
  - 36 did not integrate by day seven
- 104 eligible starts
  - 82 created a workspace
  - 22 did not create a workspace
- Support:
  - eligible-Start support incidence uses all mature eligible starts
  - post-workspace support uses mature created workspaces
  - routed-before-setup workload is reported separately

The headline should therefore be something like:

“Among mature eligible Helio Start starts, 68/104 reached first integration by day seven; 36/104 remained nonactivating at day seven. Support incidence is measured against all eligible starts, with post-workspace support shown separately against created workspaces. Routed-before-setup cases remain visible in the 16/120 intake-routing panel.”

Finally, Helio Start must remain its own cohort, keyed from the Start eligibility/entitlement state at entry. input.title: Helio lifecycle design lineage — 2028-01-01
input.body:
Design lineage note — 2028-01-01

These are two separate threads. The onboarding-trigger change altered lifecycle delivery behavior; the activation review altered measurement direction. They should not be treated as one combined change.

1. Onboarding email trigger change
The fixed calendar-day-7 onboarding touch was changed to an activation-triggered path for the defined treated mid-segment: users not activated at calendar day 7 received the touch when they crossed activation, with duplicate-send and event-eligibility protection. The change suppressed only the fixed day-7 touch; it did not change controls, users already activated before day 7, users outside the segment, or other lifecycle touches. The resulting successor behavior is represented by Activation-triggered onboarding touch v2; the earlier day-7 trigger-condition version is decommissioned.

2. Why activation was reviewed, and the successor metric direction
Activation was reviewed separately because the prior denominator/definition could make the read misleading—especially by excluding eligible starts that had not activated or needed support before activation—and because definition drift had to be resolved for comparable reporting. The intended successor direction was to measure first supported integration within seven days divided by all eligible starts with complete seven-day windows. Keep nonactivating starts in the denominator, show still-observing starts separately, and place support-load measures beside activation rather than hiding pre-activation demand.

Boundary: the first thread is a trigger and message-timing change; the second is a metric-definition and denominator decision. Neither should be cited as evidence that the other caused or required it.

input.body:
Date: April 17, 2023

The temporary dip in the second post-ship cohort was a one-time artifact caused by an outage in the CS auto-onboarding-nudge system. The outage lasted approximately 36 hours. During that window, affected mid-segment accounts activated later than expected, shifting the timing represented in the cohort and bringing week-1 retention to +1.4 points versus baseline rather than the stronger result seen in the preceding post-ship read.

This was not a failure of lifecycle_onboarding_trigger_v2 or its conversion logic. The downstream activation-event email continued to send, but at a different point relative to the rest of the onboarding flow. After the incident, the CS nudge was back up and the lifecycle system was operating normally; subsequent monitoring showed the cohort curve recovering without evidence of a durable regression. The incident is therefore recorded as a temporary timing artifact, not a change in the underlying onboarding-trigger result.

input.title: July 2023 decision rights — Helio Start and retained-mid expansion
input.body:
PERIOD-SPECIFIC HISTORICAL RECORD — JULY 2023
This note records the July 2023 working arrangement for the governance retrospective. It was an informal reuse of an investigation framework, not a permanent org chart, formal company process, or statement of current org policy.

Scope and separation
- Helio Start: guarded pre-discovery for the self-serve operating model. It was not a launch path, Q3 revenue commitment, or forecast.
- Retained-mid expansion: Expansion Assist / the retained-mid expansion-nudge follow-on. The earlier nudge had not cleared the bar for a blanket retained-mid rollout; the follow-on remained separate, exploratory, and behavior-based.
- The two workstreams had separate populations, readouts, and decision language. Neither was evidence for the other, and no blended totals or progress conclusions were intended.

Strategic decision lane
- Riley owned the decision rules, executive tradeoffs, and cross-functional guardrails for both lanes.
- For Helio Start, strategic continuation required the eligibility/refusal, instrumentation, lifecycle, and support gates to be understood and cleared. Any August beta discussion was conditional on those gates; it was not a launch approval.
- For retained-mid expansion, the strategic boundary was to reject a blanket rollout or forecast treatment while allowing focused, behavior-based exploration and measurement.
- Decisions to change scope, cross the gates, frame work as launch/rollout or forecast, or combine evidence across lanes belonged in this strategic lane.

Routine execution lane
- Owen owned first-pass readout shapes: the Helio Start baseline/candidate field-completeness cuts and the retained-mid expansion eligibility and measurement cuts, with samples, caveats, and unusable evidence called out.
- Ines owned lifecycle-fork risk maps and copy boundaries for both workstreams, including keeping state-changing lifecycle work out of scope until the relevant gates cleared.
- Routine execution could prepare measurements, document assumptions, and surface risks; it could not change eligibility, launch/rollout status, forecast treatment, or the separation between the lanes without a strategic decision.

Retrospective interpretation
The July arrangement deliberately separated strategic judgment from evidence-gathering and risk-mapping execution. Treat the ownership and boundaries above as a record of how decisions were handled during July 2023 only—not as current organizational policy.

input.title: CS auto-nudge — first-live control-evidence scorecard
input.body:
CONTROL-EVIDENCE SCORECARD

Scope
- Control: first-live CS auto-nudge operating ledger
- Ledger status: CLOSED
- Primary denominator: unique evaluated decisions
- Evidence boundary: first-live review result; not a mature-reliability or zero-error claim

1. QUANTITATIVE RECONCILIATION

Measure                                      Count     Reconciliation / treatment
Unique evaluated decisions                   1,184     Primary denominator
Failed-closed: stale or conflicting             53     Held closed; included once in denominator
Handled using current state                  1,131     Proceeded or suppressed using current state
Primary-denominator check                    1,184     53 + 1,131 = 1,184; no residual

Outcome classification rule
- Failed closed means the decision did not proceed on stale or conflicting required state.
- Current-state handling means the decision proceeded or was suppressed using current state after the applicable evaluation.
- Holds and fresh-check outcomes remain in audit history; they do not create additional primary-denominator rows.

2. FAILED-CLOSED DECISIONS

Control result: 53 stale or conflicting decisions failed closed.
- Safety behavior: no stale or conflicting decision was allowed to proceed on the affected state.
- Audit treatment: one primary ledger row per unique scheduled decision; hold reason, fresh check, and final disposition retained in audit history.
- Do not combine this count with current-state outcomes or count a reevaluation as a second decision.

3. CURRENT-STATE DECISIONS

Control result: 1,131 decisions proceeded or were suppressed using current state.
- This is a separate outcome class from the 53 failed-closed decisions.
- The count includes final handling after ordinary current-state evaluation; it is not a count of all intermediate holds, alerts, or fresh checks.

4. DELAYED-SOURCE SUBSET — MAY 20

Subset size: 12 decisions affected by the May 20 Customer Success source-refresh delay.
- Inclusion: all 12 are already included once in the 1,184 primary denominator and within the 53 failed-closed decisions.
- No double-counting: the 12 are a subset, not an additional category; their holds, fresh checks, and final outcomes remain audit history.
- Fresh-check outcomes: 8 suppressions and 4 proceeds.
- Customer-safety result: no stale-state nudge and no customer correction.

5. CROSS-SURFACE AGREEMENT

Governed field                          Status differences
External-system authority               0
Connector authentication                0
Entitlement                             0
Qualifying human admin                  0
Customer Success work                   0

Agreement result
- 0 of 1,184 evaluated decisions had a different governed-field status between the corresponding reporting and lifecycle views.
- All five governed fields agreed across the evaluated decisions.
- This is an evidence statement about observed status agreement, not a claim that the system is error-free or permanently reliable.

6. CUSTOMER-CORRECTION OUTCOME

- Customer corrections required: 0.
- No customer correction was required for the evaluated ledger decisions, including the 12 May 20 delayed-source decisions.
- This result does not authorize customer contact or substitute for an incident-stop decision if later evidence changes.

7. EXTERNAL-SYSTEM AUTHORITY — NARROW DEFINITION

For this scorecard, external-system authority means only verified readiness to perform the connector’s required owner-level permission or network-allowlist action.

It does not mean:
- permission to contact customers;
- approval to send an automated nudge;
- consent, eligibility, entitlement, or Customer Success-work clearance;
- authority to change customer state or override a failed-closed decision.

Automated customer contact requires its own applicable messaging, eligibility, and operational controls. The shared-state evidence and connector readiness must not be read as contact authorization.

8. CONTROL OWNERSHIP AND REVIEW USE

- Routine operating explanation and exception ledger: Owen.
- Messaging-state alignment: Ines.
- Engineering release and rollback control: Daniela.
- Disputed semantics, cross-surface consequences, customer-correction and incident-stop decisions, and executive claims: Riley.
- Review use: retain the unique-decision denominator, field-specific holds, delayed-source audit trail, cross-surface comparison, and customer-correction evidence together. Do not infer causality, maturity, or permission to contact customers from this scorecard alone.

FINAL CONTROL CONCLUSION

PASS WITH EVIDENCE LIMITS: 1,184 unique decisions reconcile exactly; 53 stale/conflicting decisions failed closed; 1,131 were proceeded or suppressed using current state; the 12-decision May 20 delayed-source subset is included once and separately traceable; all five governed fields agreed across reporting and lifecycle views; and no customer correction was required.

Separately, 2025 Part D has a $2,000 annual out-of-pocket threshold for covered Part D drugs.[6] That is not a prediction of Mom’s spending and is not a complete annual budget: premiums, non-covered drugs, and costs outside covered Part D benefits may be treated separately.

Document checklist

Obtain these documents for Mom’s current plan and each plan being considered:

[ ] Complete 2025 Annual Notice of Change, including attachments, plan name, contract/PBP number, and effective date.

[ ] 2025 Evidence of Coverage. This provides the detailed rules, covered benefits, cost-sharing, exceptions, and member obligations.[2]

[ ] 2025 Summary of Benefits or benefit chart, if available.

[ ] Final 2025 formulary. For every medication, record:
- Exact name, strength, dosage form, and quantity
- Tier
- Whether the deductible applies
- Copay or coinsurance before and after the deductible
- Prior authorization, step therapy, quantity limits, or specialty-pharmacy requirements

Medicare recommends checking the formulary before joining a plan.[4]

[ ] Complete 2025 Pharmacy Directory. Mark:
- Mom’s usual pharmacy
- A backup pharmacy
- Mail-order pharmacy
- Pharmacies near home and any regular travel locations
- Which locations are preferred and which are merely in-network

[ ] Premium billing notice or statement showing the gross premium, subsidies, penalties, adjustments, and actual payment method.

[ ] Any Extra Help/LIS, Medicaid, Medicare Savings Program, employer/union, VA, or state-assistance notices.

[ ] Mom’s complete medication list, including occasional prescriptions, insulin, specialty drugs, vaccines, and drugs obtained through a doctor’s office where relevant.

[ ] Last year’s pharmacy receipts and Explanation of Benefits statements, preferably covering a full 12 months.

[ ] A Medicare Plan Finder comparison using Mom’s ZIP code, exact medications, quantities, expected fills, and each pharmacy she might use. Medicare’s comparison tool supports using saved drugs and pharmacies.[5]

[ ] If this is Medicare Advantage rather than a standalone Part D plan, the plan’s 2025 health-coverage Evidence of Coverage and medical out-of-pocket limit as well.

Questions to ask each plan

1. “Is $28.90 the gross premium or Mom’s actual net premium? Does it include or exclude Extra Help, penalties, or income-related adjustments?”

2. “For each of Mom’s prescriptions, is it covered in 2025? What are the exact tier, deductible treatment, copay or coinsurance, and estimated 30-day and 90-day costs?”

3. “What would each prescription cost at her usual pharmacy, a preferred pharmacy, a non-preferred in-network pharmacy, and mail order?”

4. “Are any medications subject to prior authorization, step therapy, quantity limits, specialty-pharmacy rules, or required generic or biosimilar substitution?”

5. “Will any existing prior authorization or exception carry over into 2025? If not, what must her prescriber submit?”

6. “Does the $590 deductible apply to every medication? Are any drugs or categories treated differently?”

7. “Which pharmacies are preferred, and is Mom’s pharmacy confirmed as preferred in the effective 2025 directory?”

8. “Are any of her medications being removed, moved to a higher tier, or subjected to new restrictions?”

9. “Please provide a written estimate based on Mom’s exact medication list and pharmacy, showing annual premium plus expected drug costs.” Ask for both:
- An ordinary-use estimate
- A high-cost scenario

10. “Is Mom receiving or eligible for Extra Help, Medicaid, a Medicare Savings Program, or state pharmaceutical assistance, and how would that change her actual 2025 costs?”

11. “Is the Medicare Prescription Payment Plan available, and which costs would remain outside it?” Treat this as a payment-scheduling option, not a discount.

12. “If Mom changes plans, when will coverage begin, and could the change affect retiree, employer, union, or other health coverage?” During the ordinary annual enrollment period, plan changes made October 15 through December 7 generally begin January 1.[5]

Use this comparison format

Plan | Net annual premium | Deductible | Annual cost for each drug | Preferred-pharmacy total | Mail-order total | Restrictions | Ordinary annual estimate | High-cost estimate

Use identical medications, quantities, fill frequency, pharmacy assumptions, and a 12-month period for every plan. The cheapest premium is not necessarily the cheapest plan overall.

input.title: Right Ankle Reassessment — November 5, 2027
input.body:
Right Ankle Reassessment and Running Plan

Date of reassessment: November 5, 2027
Scheduled visit: 8:30–9:15 a.m. Central

Reason for reassessment
Review of the right-ankle running rehabilitation record and determination of whether to progress beyond the 35-minute running limit.

Pre-assessment rehabilitation record
Eight 35-minute runs were completed on October 2, 6, 10, 13, 16, 18, 22, and 27, 2027. The first seven were symptom-free. The following-day check after the October 27 run was subsequently completed without focal ankle pain, swelling, instability, gait change, or symptoms during ordinary walking or stairs.

Reassessment findings
The clinician reviewed the symptom-free record. Examination found:
- No focal tenderness.
- No swelling.
- No instability.
- No gait change.

Authorized plan
- Running: Cleared for two nonconsecutive 40-minute continuous easy runs per week.
- Bike commuting: Tuesday and Thursday remain the only authorized bike-commute days. Each leg is capped at 25 minutes at easy effort.
- Run/bike separation: No running on a bike-commute day.
- Strengthening: Continue ankle-and-calf strengthening three times per week.
- Monitoring: Check symptoms during each session and again the following day.
- Progression rule: Advance only when symptoms remain absent both during the session and through the following day.

Not authorized
- A third weekly run.
- Any additional bike-commute day.
- Any progression beyond the stated duration or intensity without further clinical authorization.

Record status
This is a clinician-facing summary of the November 5, 2027 reassessment and the activity plan reported as authorized at that visit.

sources.label: Assistant's reply to Riley Tanaka, message 002748
excerpts:
to verify before choosing

1. Fee timing and refund
   - Exact annual-fee posting date.
   - Whether the fee is refundable after a product change.
   - The issuer’s downgrade/refund window—often expressed as a number of days after posting.
   - Whether the refund is full, prorated, or unavailable after that window.
   - Whether the fee can be waived or offset with a retention offer.

2. Product-change mechanics
   - Whether this is a true product change rather than a new account.
   - Whether the account number, credit line, account age, and payment history remain intact.
   - Whether there is a hard credit inquiry.
   - Whether autopay, recurring charges, digital-wallet tokens, and authorized users carry over.
   - Whether the change can be reversed later.

3. Points
   - Whether the existing points remain intact immediately after the change.
   - Whether points must be redeemed or transferred first.
   - Whether the points balance, transfer partners, redemption rates, or expiration rules change.
   - Whether any points or rewards can be clawed back because of the downgrade.

4. No-fee card rewards
   - Exact definition of “1.5x travel/dining.”
   - Whether travel includes transit, rideshare, hotels, rental cars, and third-party booking sites.
   - Whether there are caps, exclusions, rotating categories, or redemption restrictions.
   - The actual redemption value and whether travel redemptions require an issuer portal.
   - Foreign-transaction fees.

5. $75 travel credit
   - Eligible merchants and transaction types.
   - Whether it is based on a calendar year, cardmember year, or statement year.
   - Whether enrollment is required.
   - Whether credits are automatic and how long they take to post.
   - Whether unused credit expires.
   - What happens if a qualifying purchase is refunded or partially refunded.

6. Lounge passes
   - Which lounges and networks accept them.
   - Whether each pass covers only the cardholder or also a guest.
   - Whether taxes, reservations, or capacity restrictions apply.
   - Expiration dates and whether unused passes are forfeited after a product change.
   - Whether access depends on holding the original card on the date of entry.

7. Benefits lost on downgrade
   - Trip cancellation/interruption and delay coverage.
   - Rental-car coverage.
   - Baggage protection.
   - Purchase protection, return protection, and extended warranty.
   - Cellphone protection, concierge, hotel status, or other card-linked benefits.
   - Whether benefits remain available for purchases made before the product change.

8. Account and credit consequences
   - Any change to APR, minimum payment, credit-line terms, or penalty fees.
   - Whether the no-fee product has a different balance-transfer or cash-advance schedule.
   - Whether the issuer will close the account instead of converting it.
   - Whether a separate application is required.

results.content:
October growth close — business read

Data pull status

- The service has no MRR, ARR-by-segment, or mid-segment churn snapshot for October 30 or October 31, 2023.
- Its undated “latest” MRR record is January 31, 2026, so I did not use it as October evidence. That record is $4.0M MRR / $48.0M ARR, with $320K net-new, $95K expansion, and $41K churned MRR.
- The connected recent-churn queries returned zero mid-segment event rows for 30, 60, and 90 days. That means no rows were returned—not that churn was zero.

October close context

- October 30 MTD company MRR: $1.575M
- ARR: $18.9M
- Net-new MRR: $64K
- Expansion MRR: $41K
- Churned MRR: $33K
- Expansion exceeded churn by $8K, before considering net-new.

The October working record shows retained-mid at $7.4M ARR across 182 accounts. That is roughly 39% of the $18.9M company ARR. However, this does not reconcile to the latest validated segment table, which totals $18.7M:

- Enterprise: $9.1M / 48.7%
- Growth: $5.6M / 29.9%
- Retained-mid: $3.4M / 18.2%
- Starter: $0.6M / 3.2%

I would not combine those two tables as though they were one clean snapshot. The difference appears to reflect segment taxonomy/versioning; the $18.7M table is the latest validated full segment breakdown, while the $7.4M retained-mid figure is the October close context. input.title: Historical Decision Rule: Onboarding Timing vs. Customer Success Coverage
input.body:
Date of record: February 10, 2023

Historical decision rule

The investigation treated onboarding timing as hypothesis #3 and the Customer Success coverage gap as hypothesis #4. Evidence that late-December or early-January starts were converting to churn on a lag would raise the priority of the onboarding-timing hypothesis and cause the Customer Success coverage hypothesis to be deprioritized—described contemporaneously as its priority “basically” dropping if #3 started to confirm.

Conversely, if onboarding-timing evidence did not begin to confirm, the Customer Success coverage hypothesis would remain on the board for investigation rather than being dropped. This was a prioritization rule for the investigation, not a conclusion that Customer Success coverage had been disproven.

Context

- The initial hypothesis order was: #1 pricing artifact, #2 competitor cycle, #3 onboarding timing, and #4 CS coverage gap.
- The onboarding-timing check was expected to become clearer around February 28.
- By February 21, competitor-cycle and generic-seasonal explanations had been ruled out, leaving onboarding timing and CS coverage as the two remaining hypotheses.
- The rule was to avoid treating preliminary onboarding evidence as conclusive; the evidence had to start to confirm before materially lowering the priority of CS coverage.

Source basis

- Riley Tanaka, February 10, 2023: “CS coverage investigation priority: basically drops if #3 starts to confirm.”
- Riley Tanaka, February 8, 2023: numbered the hypotheses with onboarding timing as #3 and CS coverage gap as #4.
- Riley Tanaka, February 21, 2023: recorded that H3 onboarding timing and H4 CS coverage remained after competitor-cycle and generic-seasonal explanations were ruled out.

input.body:
HISTORICAL SETUP — NOT A CURRENT CONCLUSION

H2 question
Could the mid-segment churn spike be explained by normal February seasonality or a competitor-cycle event?

Planned test (before the ruling)
- Use the same cohort logic as the January scan and Owen’s validation check.
- Compare same-window February churn for the mid-segment, keeping segment definition and denominator handling consistent.
- Line up historical same-window churn by segment and place the current read beside prior February comparators.
- Overlay dated market events and only competitor activity that could be independently timestamped.
- Where the data supported it, report p-values and effect size.
- Perform a final denominator-handling sanity check before calling the result.

Interpretation rule
A comparable historical spike, aligned with a dated market or competitor event, would support H2; ordinary historical levels without a matching spike would weaken it. Treat missing historical snapshots or untimestamped competitor evidence as measurement gaps—not as confirming evidence.

Keep Marcus’s pricing-page experiment separate from this H2 cut so parallel-test noise does not contaminate the investigation read.

Archive status

Prep notes

Core framing

This is not a pricing-only decision. It is a product, operations, support, and sales-boundary decision. The question is whether we can offer a repeatable sub-50-seat product without letting every small account become a bespoke 200-seat implementation.

Recommended boundary

Sub-50 means 49 paid seats or fewer. Keep 50–75 in the starter framing; do not blur it into the 75–200 mid-segment definition.

Supportable in a Q3 launch

- Fixed seat cap and fixed entitlements
- Standard plan and billing flow
- Standard workspace and permission model
- Standard onboarding path with documentation and lightweight assistance
- Standard support channel and response expectations
- Standard import path where the product already supports it
- Clear upgrade path when the account outgrows the tier
- Sales can sell only what is in the published package

Custom-small-account pain / refuse by default

- Custom invoicing or contract terms
- Migration or data-cleaning services
- Bespoke permissions or workspace limits
- Dedicated onboarding or implementation help
- SSO/SCIM, audit-log, or other enterprise controls unless already productized for this tier
